Photograph: Balazs Toth/Mezőkövesd Képekben/Reuters Hungary Bus carrying Polish pilgrims crashes in Hungary, leaving 12 dead Another 10 people in serious condition after bus veers off motorway and overturns Jakub Krupa and agencies Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.07 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Twelve people have died after a bus carrying a group of Polish tourists overturned on the M3 motorway in Hungary on the way back from Bosnia and Herzegovina . Local police said the bus crashed near the town of Mezőkeresztes after it “went off the straight road into a ditch and overturned” at 1am local time. Early reports suggested the driver had probably fallen asleep. He survived the crash and was taken into custody. The bus was carrying a group of pilgrims from Poland’s south-eastern Podkarpackie region who were returning from a pilgrimage to the Catholic shrine in Međugorje, in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina, with 57 passengers and two drivers onboard. Poland’s foreign ministry said “virtually all” passengers were transferred to local hospitals in Eger, Debrecen and Miskolc, and 10 people were in a serious condition. The Hungarian ambulance service said 37 people sustained minor injuries. Polish and Hungarian leaders expressed their condolences after the crash. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, said: “With deep sorrow, I received the tragic news of the accident involving a Polish bus in Hungary , in which so many of our compatriots perished. “In the face of this unimaginable tragedy, which has touched us all, I join in prayer and profound compassion with the families and loved ones of the victims.” View image in fullscreen A crane lifts the bus from the side of the motorway. Photograph: Zoltán Máthé/EPA Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar, expressed his “sincere condolences to the families of the victims” and thanked the emergency services involved in the rescue operation. Poland’s infrastructure minister, Dariusz Klimczak, said the general inspectorate of road transport would conduct enhanced checks on all buses and drivers’ working hours. The owner of the bus company involved in the crash told Business Insider Polska that the vehicle “was driven by two experienced drivers”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion The investigation into the crash will be led by a group of Polish prosecutors from the south-eastern town of Krosno, the prosecutors’ office said in a statement. Međugorje, despite some doubts about its religious history , is a popular summer destination for Polish Catholics. In 2022, 12 people died and 30 were injured when a bus carrying Polish pilgrims to Međugorje crashed in Croatia . In 2002, 20 Polish pilgrims died and 31 were injured in a bus crash in Hungary. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-to-close-br.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KhS1 The Goethe-Institut offers courses in German language and culture Image: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS Advertisement Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Thursday that Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centers would be closed in Russia. In remarks carried by Russian news agencies TASS and Interfax, Lavrov said Goethe-Institut branches would be closed in the Russian cities of Moscow, St. Petersburg and Yekaterinburg. The statement came after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted ‌drone ⁠attack at ⁠the Leipzig/Halle Airport. Germany's response to that incident included closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn. 'End' of German cultural presence in Russia "Of course they will be closed after our cultural center was expelled from there [from Berlin]," Lavrov said, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok. "They deliberately took this step — they could not have failed to understand — which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia," Lavrov said, according to state news agency TASS. He added the centers had remained open "despite all the Ukrainian complications in our relations with the West." What did Germany say? Berlin said it regretted Russia's decision, calling it unjustified and damaging. "The Goethe-Institut ... has played an important role in Russia as a cultural bridge, and we would have been prepared to continue that," German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters on Thursday. He noted that there had "generally always been a good relationship" between the people of Russia and Germany. The "problem," rather, was the Russian leadership, he added. The foreign minister said Germany and its partners have "always been prepared to engage in a reasonable dialogue with Russia," but stressed that a "prerequisite for this is that Russia finally puts an end to its war of aggression against Ukraine and, above all, refrains from all attacks of any kind against us and our allies." He said closing branches of the Goethe-Institut as payback for Berlin's closure of the Russian House was unjustified, as the German government's step had been in response to a clear act of aggression by Russia. Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Russia has also threatened to take further measures, possibly including the closure of Germany's consulate general in St. Petersburg. On Wednesday, Russia's Foreign Ministry summoned the charge d'affaires of the German Embassy in Moscow to protest Berlin's response to the August drone incident . According to the ministry, the official was called in over what it described as anti-Russian actions and statements by the German leadership. On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Moscow for the explosives-laden drone. What is the Goethe-Institut? The cultural organization operates in around 100 countries worldwide, promoting the study of the German language and providing information about German culture and society. Russia's first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, shortly after the collapse of the Soviet Union . The Goethe-Institut is one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia. In 2018, Russia ordered the closure of the British Council following a diplomatic dispute with the UK. https://www.politico.eu/sponsored-conten.text: As Europe plans its response to the neurological disease burden, a fundamental measurement gap is being overlooked — and the cost of ignoring it is being felt. A briefing requested earlier this year by the European Parliament’s Committee on Public Health (SANT) put it plainly: neurological diseases are one of Europe’s most urgent and rapidly expanding health, social and economic challenges. Published in February 2026, it calls for a coordinated European plan linking prevention, early diagnosis, research and innovation. 1 But before Europe considers what that plan should look like, a foundational question demands attention: are we measuring the right things? Multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic, progressive disease of the central nervous system that disrupts communication between the brain and the body, offers a revealing case study. Consider a woman in her mid-30s, working, raising a family, managing what her neurologist calls “stable” MS. She has not slept properly in years, her memory has been slipping and she is cutting her hours at work. Her last clinical note reads: “No change.” On paper, she is stable, but in reality she is anything but. Advertisement Her story is not unusual. According to research commissioned by Sanofi * , the gap between what health systems measure and what people with MS experience may be costing individuals, families and economies more than we realize. 3 The stakes for Europe Over 3 million people globally live with MS and Europe has the highest prevalence, at 133 per 100,000 people. 2,3 The condition strikes primarily during prime working years, meaning hundreds of thousands of people are navigating a progressive, unpredictable disease at precisely the point when inadequate support is felt most acutely. 3 That support begins with measurement. And right now, the tools used to assess MS in clinical practice do not fully capture what people with the disease experience. 3 The consequences extend far beyond the clinic: 82 percent of people with severe MS rely on unpaid family caregiving, yet this burden rarely appears in standard health data or policy design. 3 When the full impact of disease is not measured, health systems can underestimate need, delay support, and overlook the wider effects on work, welfare and family life. 3 The measurement gap Advertisement The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), the primary tool used to measure MS disability, was developed in 1983 to assess walking ability. We now know that MS affects far more than mobility. Fatigue affects 94 percent of people with MS, while 75 percent report cognitive difficulties, but both are absent in the EDSS assessment. 3 In a field where clinical consensus is rare, seven in ten neurologists agree: a more comprehensive approach is needed. 3 Growing recognition of smouldering neuroinflammation has made the need for new methods of quantifying MS progression increasingly urgent. This slow, chronic disease activity can persist even when a patient appears clinically stable, with effects that are subtle, cumulative and easy to miss until significant damage has already occurred. 4 This is why Sanofi initiated the development of the Smouldering Associated Worsening (SAW) Index + . The SAW Index Study — led by an international steering committee of leading MS clinicians, researchers and patient advocates — is due to complete in 2027. Based on hundreds of hours of in-depth qualitative research with people with MS, the goal of the SAW Index is to provide neurologists with a comprehensive measurement framework that bridges the gap between lived experience and what clinical tools are currently able to detect. According to the European Multiple Sclerosis Platform, people with MS experience an average of 14 symptoms within the first five years of diagnosis, with fatigue, sensory problems, sleep disturbances, cognitive impairment and balance problems among the most common. 5 These are precisely the experiences the SAW Index is designed to surface, replacing static labels like “moderately affected” with measurement metrics grounded in the experience and words of people with MS. The cost of this gap These aspects of MS can be challenging to quantify and are associated with substantial societal and economic burdens. Lifetime productivity loss per person with MS ranges from €394,000 in France to €668,000 in Germany. 3 The cost profile shifts significantly as the disease progresses: in mild MS, direct healthcare costs dominate; in severe MS, indirect costs become the primary driver. 3 Indeed, lost wages, absenteeism, early retirement, disability payments and the growing burden on unpaid carers outweigh medical costs in many countries, placing growing long-term pressure on social insurance and disability systems. 3 Advertisement Early identification of progression could change that trajectory, extending years of employment, preserving household income, and reducing long-term dependence on disability and social benefits. 3,6 That is a cost-avoidance opportunity current measurement frameworks are missing. Progress in motion There is no single fix, but there is momentum. MS care has advanced significantly in recent decades: diagnosis is happening earlier, treatment options have expanded and the focus is shifting from relapse control alone to slowing long-term disability progression. 7 Furthermore, there is growing recognition of the importance of cognition, mental health, rehabilitation and the day-to-day realities that shape whether people living with MS can remain independent and active. 8 The challenge now is to ensure policy keeps pace with that progress, and better measurement is part of the answer. If Europe wants health spending to deliver lasting value, it should see these improvements not as costs to be managed, but as investments in independence, participation, productivity and more sustainable health systems. Time to act Advertisement The European Parliament’s SANT Committee has called for a fully funded European neurological health plan — one with the scale and ambition of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan, aligning health, research and societal action in a unified framework. 1 MS offers a clear and immediate test case for what that ambition looks like in practice. But ambitious plans require accurate data. If Europe is serious about a coordinated response to neurological disease, getting measurement right is not a secondary concern; it is the foundation on which everything else depends. The people living with MS across the continent cannot wait for the tools that measure their disease to catch up with the science that understands it.
